stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the team's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Many songbirds in cities begin their dawn chorus earlier than birds of the same species in forests. Because cities are both louder and brighter than forests, the cause has been hard to pin down. To separate the two factors, ornithologist Lena Achterberg and colleagues recorded European robins at forest sites and at urban sites. In each habitat, half of the sites were lit at night by streetlights. The team hypothesizes that artificial light, rather than urban conditions in general, causes the earlier start.

Mean Start of Dawn Song (minutes before sunrise)
Habitat | Unlit sites | Lit sites
Forest | 18 | 41
Urban | 20 | 43
choices: Robins at lit urban sites began singing 43 minutes before sunrise, earlier than the robins in any other group.
Unlit urban and unlit forest sites differed by only 2 minutes, while lit sites in each habitat started over 20 minutes earlier.
Robins at lit forest sites began singing later than robins at unlit urban sites, which started 20 minutes before sunrise.
Robins at lit sites sang for more minutes each morning than robins at unlit sites, whether in forests or in cities.
explanation: The hypothesis separates light from urban conditions, so you need two comparisons. With light held constant (unlit sites), city and forest differ by just 2 minutes (20 vs. 18). With habitat held constant, adding light moves the start more than 20 minutes earlier (18 to 41 in forests, 20 to 43 in cities). Light makes the difference and habitat barely does, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: This is accurate, but lit urban sites are both lit and urban, so this one value can't show which factor is responsible. You chose a true statement that doesn't make the comparison the hypothesis requires.

C.why: Lit forest robins started 41 minutes before sunrise, which is earlier than the unlit urban robins at 20 minutes, not later. You may have read a bigger number as a later time, when the column counts minutes before sunrise.

D.why: The table shows only when singing began, not how long it lasted. You attributed to the data a measurement it doesn't contain.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Ibarra's conclusion?
stimulus:
Along rocky coasts, sea otters prey on sea urchins, and urchins graze on kelp. Ecologists therefore expect otters to benefit kelp indirectly, by reducing urchin numbers. If that chain explains otters' effect, the benefit should be large where urchins are abundant and small where urchins are scarce, since there otters have few grazers to remove. Marine ecologist Tomás Ibarra surveyed reefs of both kinds, with and without resident otters, and concluded that otters' effect on kelp depends on urchin abundance.

Mean Kelp Density (stipes per square meter)
Reef type | Otters absent | Otters present
Urchin-rich | 2 | 11
Urchin-poor | 9 | 10
choices: On reefs with otters present, kelp density was nearly the same on urchin-rich reefs (11) and urchin-poor reefs (10).
On reefs without otters, urchin-poor reefs had far more kelp than urchin-rich reefs had, 9 versus 2 stipes.
Otters raised kelp density from 2 to 11 on urchin-rich reefs but only from 9 to 10 on urchin-poor reefs.
On urchin-poor reefs, the presence of otters raised kelp density more than it did on urchin-rich reefs.
explanation: The conclusion is about the size of the otter effect, so first compare otters absent with otters present within each reef type, then compare those two changes. On urchin-rich reefs, kelp density rises by 9 stipes. On urchin-poor reefs, it rises by 1. A large effect where urchins are abundant and almost none where they're scarce is the predicted pattern.

A.why: This is accurate, but it compares the two reef types only when otters are present, so it never measures what otters change. You compared the wrong cells.

B.why: This is accurate and shows that urchins reduce kelp, but it looks only at reefs without otters. It says nothing about whether otters' effect depends on urchins. You supported a nearby point instead of the one the conclusion makes.

D.why: Otters raised kelp by only 1 stipe on urchin-poor reefs, compared with 9 on urchin-rich reefs. You reversed the direction of the comparison.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the coaches' claim?
stimulus:
In road cycling, climbing speed depends less on total power than on power relative to body mass, expressed in watts per kilogram. A coaching team split 24 amateur cyclists into two groups of similar ability. For ten weeks, one group trained with heavy resistance work and the other with short, intense intervals; all other training was identical. The team then measured each rider's body mass and sustained power. The coaches claim that interval training produced the better climbers, even though it yielded lower total power.

Mean Results After Ten Weeks
Training group | Body mass (kg) | Sustained power (watts)
Heavy resistance | 80 | 320
Intense intervals | 60 | 270
choices: The interval group averaged 4.5 watts per kilogram, compared with 4.0 watts per kilogram for the resistance group.
The resistance group sustained an average of 320 watts, which is 50 watts more than the interval group sustained.
The interval group's riders weighed an average of 20 kilograms less than the resistance group's riders weighed.
The resistance group averaged more watts per kilogram of body mass than the interval group averaged after training.
explanation: The passage says climbing depends on watts per kilogram, so you have to compute that ratio for each group: 270 ÷ 60 = 4.5 for intervals and 320 ÷ 80 = 4.0 for resistance. The interval group comes out ahead on the measure that predicts climbing, even with lower raw power, which matches the claim.

B.why: This is accurate, but it uses raw power. The passage says raw power is not what decides climbing, and the claim expects the interval group to have less of it. You read the raw values instead of computing the ratio the passage defined.

C.why: Body mass is only half of the ratio. A lighter rider climbs better only if their power doesn't drop too much. You stopped after one part of the calculation.

D.why: The resistance group averaged 4.0 W/kg, which is lower than the interval group's 4.5. You may have assumed that more total watts means more watts per kilogram.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Okafor's conclusion?
stimulus:
In many maritime and farming traditions, work songs use call-and-response: a leader sings a line and the group answers. Ethnomusicologist Adaeze Okafor examined 400 transcribed work songs. She sorted them by the size of the crew that sang them and by whether the task they accompanied, such as hauling a rope, required workers to move in unison. Okafor concludes that larger crews favored call-and-response, but only for tasks that demanded synchronized movement.

Share of Song Lines in Call-and-Response Form (%)
Crew size | Synchronized tasks | Unsynchronized tasks
Small (2–4 workers) | 30 | 25
Large (10 or more workers) | 70 | 27
choices: Large crews doing synchronized tasks used call-and-response in 70% of lines, the highest share of any group.
For both synchronized and unsynchronized tasks, large crews used call-and-response far more than small crews.
Small crews used call-and-response at similar rates for synchronized and unsynchronized tasks, 30% and 25%.
For synchronized tasks, the share rose from 30% to 70% with crew size; for other tasks, it barely changed.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts: crew size raises call-and-response for synchronized tasks, and it doesn't for unsynchronized ones. You need the crew-size comparison in both columns. It's 30% to 70% for synchronized tasks and 25% to 27% for unsynchronized ones, which is the 'only for' pattern.

A.why: This is accurate, but a single top value doesn't show a crew-size effect, and it doesn't address the condition that the effect appears only for synchronized tasks. You picked the most striking number instead of the comparison the claim requires.

B.why: For unsynchronized tasks, the share went from only 25% to 27%, which is not 'far more.' This choice also states the broad version of the claim and drops the 'only for synchronized tasks' limit Okafor sets.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares task types within small crews only, so crew size never varies. You compared the wrong pair of cells.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Castellanos's hypothesis?
stimulus: Folklorists have long debated why oral tales become more uniform over time. Rhea Castellanos studied one widespread tale, counting how many distinct endings appeared among variants collected in coastal and inland villages in the 1880s and in the 1950s. Printed tale collections reached the coastal villages around 1900 but did not circulate inland until the 1970s. Castellanos hypothesizes that printed collections reduced the variety of endings by giving tellers a single fixed version to imitate.

figure.caption: Distinct Endings Among Recorded Variants of the Tale
figure.alt: Bar graph showing the number of distinct tale endings for coastal and inland villages in the 1880s and the 1950s.

choices: In the 1880s, coastal and inland villages had the same number of distinct endings, with 12 recorded in each.
Coastal villages fell from 12 distinct endings to 4, while inland villages fell only from 12 to 10.
Inland villages had fewer distinct endings in the 1950s than in the 1880s, dropping from 12 to 10.
Coastal villages had more distinct endings in the 1950s than inland villages had in the 1950s.
explanation: Use the passage to decide the direction first. Between the 1880s and the 1950s, only the coastal villages had print, so if print reduced variety, endings should drop sharply on the coast and change little inland. The coast falls from 12 to 4, while inland falls only from 12 to 10. That contrast links the decline to print.

A.why: This is accurate, but it describes only the starting point, before print arrived anywhere. A shared baseline doesn't show what print did. You chose a true statement that doesn't test the hypothesis.

C.why: This is accurate, but the inland villages never had print during this period. Their small decline is the comparison group, not the effect of print. You read the wrong pair of bars.

D.why: In the 1950s, coastal villages had 4 distinct endings and inland villages had 10, so the coast had fewer, not more. You reversed the comparison.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus:
Adjuvants are substances added to vaccines to provoke a stronger immune reaction. Because the immune system weakens with age, older animals often respond poorly to a vaccine given alone. Immunologist Rana Okafor and colleagues vaccinated young and old mice, either with or without an adjuvant, and four weeks later measured antibody levels in the animals' blood. The researchers hypothesized that the adjuvant would increase antibody levels by a greater amount in old mice than in young mice.

Mean Antibody Level Four Weeks After Vaccination (units per milliliter)
Age group | Without adjuvant | With adjuvant
Young | 40 | 60
Old | 15 | 45
choices: Among mice given the adjuvant, young mice had antibody levels 15 units higher than old mice did.
The adjuvant raised antibody levels by 30 units in old mice but by only 20 units in young mice.
The adjuvant raised antibody levels by 30 units in young mice but by only 20 units in old mice.
The adjuvant raised old mice's antibody levels by 30 units, to match young mice given the adjuvant.
explanation: The hypothesis is about the size of the adjuvant's effect in each age group, so you need two gaps. For each row, subtract the 'without' number from the 'with' number. For old mice the gap is 45 − 15 = 30. For young mice it is 60 − 40 = 20. A gain of 30 is bigger than a gain of 20, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts, so this choice supports it.

A.why: The number is right (60 − 45 = 15), but you compared the wrong cells. This compares the two age groups within one column. The hypothesis is about how much the adjuvant changes each group's level, so you need the gap within each row.

C.why: You worked out the right two gaps but gave them to the wrong groups. The table shows a 20-unit gain for young mice and a 30-unit gain for old mice, not the other way around.

D.why: The 30-unit gain is correct, but the choice claims more than the table shows. Old mice given the adjuvant reached 45 units, still well below the 60 units of young mice given the adjuvant, so the two groups did not match.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Varga's conclusion?
stimulus:
Folklorists have long asked whether printed collections flatten regional folktales. When a tale passes by word of mouth, tellers tend to tie it to nearby places, a habit that may fade once a standard printed version circulates. Folklorist Ines Varga recorded tellings of one legend across a mountain region, noting where each teller lived, how the teller had learned the tale, and whether the telling named a local landmark. Varga concluded that how a tale is learned makes a bigger difference to landmark mentions in villages than in towns.

Tellings That Name a Local Landmark (%)
Where teller lives | Learned orally | Learned from print
Village | 72 | 30
Town | 48 | 40
choices: Among tellers who learned the tale orally, village tellings named a landmark 24 percentage points more often than town tellings did.
Orally learned tellings named a landmark 8 percentage points more often than print-learned ones in villages and 42 points more often in towns.
In both villages and towns, orally learned tellings named a landmark at least 40 percentage points more often than print-learned ones did.
Orally learned tellings named a landmark 42 percentage points more often than print-learned ones in villages but only 8 points more often in towns.
explanation: Varga's claim compares how much the way a tale is learned matters in two places. That means two gaps, one for each row. In villages, oral minus print is 72 − 30 = 42 points. In towns it is 48 − 40 = 8 points. The gap is far wider in villages, so this choice makes the comparison the conclusion needs.

A.why: The number is right (72 − 48 = 24), but you compared the wrong cells. This compares villages with towns among oral learners only. The conclusion is about the gap between oral and print learners within each place.

B.why: You found the right two gaps but swapped them. The 42-point gap belongs to villages and the 8-point gap belongs to towns, so this version turns the finding around.

C.why: You took the village result and applied it to towns too. The town gap is only 48 − 40 = 8 points, nowhere near 40.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?
stimulus:
Most printed maps put north at the top, so a traveler heading south must mentally rotate the map to decide which way to turn. Some navigation displays instead rotate the map so that the traveler's direction always points up. Cartographer Tomas Lindqvist suspected that the burden of mental rotation grows with the number of possible turns. His team had participants walk unfamiliar routes with one kind of map or the other and counted wrong turns. The researchers concluded that heading-up maps reduce errors chiefly at complex intersections.

Mean Wrong Turns per Route
Intersection type | North-up map | Heading-up map
Simple | 1.2 | 1.0
Complex | 4.6 | 2.2
choices: At complex intersections, heading-up map users made 2.4 fewer wrong turns than north-up users did, compared with 0.2 fewer at simple intersections.
At simple intersections, heading-up map users made 2.4 fewer wrong turns than north-up users did, compared with 0.2 fewer at complex intersections.
North-up map users made 3.4 more wrong turns at complex intersections than they made at simple intersections, on average, across the routes.
Heading-up map users made fewer than half as many wrong turns as north-up users did at both simple and complex intersections.
explanation: The conclusion says the heading-up map's advantage shows up mainly at complex intersections. So you need the map gap within each row. At complex intersections it is 4.6 − 2.2 = 2.4 fewer wrong turns. At simple intersections it is 1.2 − 1.0 = 0.2. Nearly all the benefit falls at complex intersections, which is what 'chiefly' requires.

B.why: You calculated both gaps correctly but gave them to the wrong intersection types. The 2.4 reduction happens at complex intersections, not simple ones.

C.why: The number is right (4.6 − 1.2 = 3.4), but it comes from the north-up column only. It shows that complex intersections cause more errors, but it says nothing about whether heading-up maps cut those errors. The conclusion depends on comparing the two maps.

D.why: You stretched the complex-intersection result to cover both rows. At complex intersections, 2.2 is less than half of 4.6. At simple intersections, though, 1.0 is nearly as high as 1.2, so the claim fails there. The conclusion itself also says the advantage is not the same everywhere.

stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to support Rautio and colleagues' hypothesis?
stimulus:
Living woody plants in cool climates tend to have leaves with toothed edges, while those in warm climates more often have smooth edges. Paleobotanists therefore use the share of toothed species in a fossil flora to estimate past temperatures. Studying four fossil sites that span a regional cooling event, Anika Rautio and colleagues hypothesized that the cooling raised the share of toothed species at inland sites but barely changed it at coastal sites, where the nearby ocean kept temperatures steady.

Share of Fossil Species with Toothed Leaf Margins (%)
Site | Before cooling | After cooling
Inland site 1 | 30 | 48
Inland site 2 | 26 | 41
Coastal site 1 | 33 | 34
Coastal site 2 | 29 | 30
choices: Inland site 1 rose from 30% to 48% toothed species, while coastal site 1 rose only from 33% to 34%.
Inland site 2 gained 15 percentage points of toothed species, while coastal site 2 gained just 1 point.
After cooling, both inland sites topped 40%, while each coastal site ended within 1 point of where it began.
Before cooling, coastal site 1 had a larger share of toothed species (33%) than inland site 1 did (30%).
explanation: The hypothesis is about change over time: inland sites should rise a lot from before to after the cooling, and coastal sites should barely move. To support it, a choice has to compare before and after for both kinds of site. Choice D reads the table correctly, but it uses only the 'Before cooling' column and compares two sites at a single moment. It says nothing about what the cooling did, so it does not support the hypothesis.

A.why: This choice gives both the before and after values for an inland site and a coastal site, and the inland site rises 18 points while the coastal site rises 1. That is exactly the contrast the hypothesis predicts. If you rejected it, you may have thought one pair of sites was too little evidence, but the question asks whether the choice uses the data to support the claim, and it does.

B.why: You have to do the subtraction yourself here: 41 − 26 = 15 and 30 − 29 = 1. Both are correct, and a large inland gain next to a tiny coastal gain supports the hypothesis. If you picked this, you probably made an arithmetic slip or expected raw table values and distrusted a computed difference.

C.why: This one looks as if it reads only the 'After cooling' column, which is the subtype's usual trap. It doesn't. 'Within 1 point of where it began' compares each coastal site with its earlier value, and both inland sites started below 30% before ending above 40%, so the before-and-after contrast is all there. You fell for the look of a single-column comparison without checking what the wording actually compares.

stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to support Ferreira's hypothesis?
stimulus:
After harvest, nitrate fertilizer left in a field can wash down past the roots and into groundwater. Because water drains quickly through the large pores of sandy soil, these losses tend to be greatest there. A winter cover crop such as cereal rye can absorb leftover nitrate before it drains away. Agronomist Tomás Ferreira therefore hypothesized that a rye cover crop would sharply reduce nitrate leaching in sandy soil but would have little effect in loam or clay.

Nitrate Lost to Leaching (kilograms per hectare)
Soil type | No cover crop | Rye cover crop
Sandy | 48 | 21
Loam | 19 | 17
Clay | 12 | 11
choices: Plots with rye lost less nitrate than plots without rye in sandy, loam, and clay soil alike.
In sandy soil, rye cut nitrate loss from 48 to 21 kg per hectare, but in loam only from 19 to 17.
Rye reduced nitrate loss by 27 kg per hectare in sandy soil but by just 1 kg per hectare in clay.
Sandy plots lost over twice as much nitrate without rye as with it, while clay plots lost about the same either way.
explanation: Ferreira's hypothesis depends on soil type: rye should make a big difference in sandy soil and only a small one in loam or clay. A supporting choice has to show that the size of rye's effect differs between soils. Choice A is accurate, but it only says rye helped somewhat everywhere. That supports a broader claim, 'rye reduces leaching', and ignores the sandy-versus-finer-soil contrast the hypothesis is about, so it does not support it.

B.why: This choice puts sandy soil (a 27-kg drop) next to loam (a 2-kg drop), which is the contrast the hypothesis predicts. If you rejected it because it leaves out clay, remember the hypothesis says 'loam or clay', so showing a small effect in loam is enough.

C.why: 48 − 21 = 27 and 12 − 11 = 1, so both numbers are right, and they show a large effect in sandy soil next to a negligible one in clay. If you picked this, you may have checked these figures against the raw table values, found neither listed, and decided the choice was inaccurate. It is computed from the table, and it is correct.

D.why: 48 is more than twice 21, and clay's 12 versus 11 is nearly unchanged, so this choice makes the soil-dependent comparison the hypothesis needs. If you thought 'over twice as much' claimed more than the table shows, check the arithmetic: 2 × 21 = 42, which is less than 48.

stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to support Haddad's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Giant planets are thought to begin as rocky cores that must grow large enough to capture gas before a young star's disk disperses. Metal-rich disks supply more solid material, so cores grow faster. Red dwarfs have small disks that sit near the limit for forming giant planets at all. Astronomer Leila Haddad therefore hypothesized that metal richness raises giant-planet rates proportionally more for red dwarfs than for Sun-like stars, as measured by each type's boost ratio: the rate among metal-rich stars divided by the rate among metal-poor stars.

Stars Hosting at Least One Giant Planet (%)
Star type | Metal-poor | Metal-rich
Sun-like | 4 | 12
Red dwarf | 1 | 5
choices: Metal-poor red dwarfs host giant planets at 1% and metal-rich ones at 5%, a boost ratio above that of Sun-like stars.
Metal richness raised the Sun-like rate by 8 percentage points but raised the red dwarf rate by only 4 points.
Metal richness made red dwarfs five times as likely to host giant planets but Sun-like stars only three times as likely.
Sun-like stars outpace red dwarfs fourfold among metal-poor stars but only 2.4-fold among metal-rich stars.
explanation: The passage defines the comparison as a ratio, so first work out each boost ratio: red dwarfs 5 ÷ 1 = 5, Sun-like stars 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The hypothesis needs the red dwarf ratio to be larger, and it is. Choice B uses raw percentage-point gains instead. Those numbers are accurate, but they make the Sun-like stars look more affected (8 points against 4), so B does not support the hypothesis. It is the raw-values trap the passage set up by defining a ratio.

A.why: This choice states the red dwarf values (1% and 5%, a ratio of 5) and says that ratio is higher than the Sun-like ratio (12 ÷ 4 = 3), which is true. If you rejected it because it gives no number for the Sun-like ratio, you needed only to check that the comparison holds, and it does.

C.why: 'Five times as likely' and 'three times as likely' are the boost ratios in plain words: 5 ÷ 1 and 12 ÷ 4. If you picked this, you probably compared raw gains (4 points against 8) and decided the choice reversed the table. The passage asks for a ratio, and by that measure this choice is right.

D.why: This looks like the subtype's wrong-series trap, because it compares the two star types instead of the two metallicity groups. But 4 ÷ 1 = 4 and 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4. If the Sun-like advantage shrinks as metallicity rises, red dwarfs must gain proportionally more, which is Haddad's hypothesis. You rejected a valid comparison because of how it was framed, without checking what it implies.
